item.title: Republican convention attendees share heartfelt tributes to late Charlie Kirk on assassination anniversary
item.description: Republicans at the GOP midterm convention in Dallas reflect on Charlie Kirk's assassination one year after the Turning Point USA founder was killed at a college event.
item.content:encoded:
A year after the shocking assassination of conservative titan and Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk, Republicans gathered at the GOP's midterm convention shared the profound ways in which the young leader and family man impacted their lives.

"Charlie Kirk is a wonderful man, and he is very much missed," Marsha Landry of Texas told Fox News Digital during an interview at the American Airlines Center, where the Republican Party is rallying to try to keep control of the House and Senate in November. "He was making a lot of progress in this country, especially among the youth. I know personally some of our children have really started paying attention."

Jacquez Jones, a young convention attendee, said Kirk's legacy lives on.

REMEMBERING CHARLIE KIRK: TURNING POINT USA'S ANDREW KOLVET REFLECTS ON CONSERVATIVE GROUP'S CHALLENGING YEAR

"It's a daily reminder that we have to have courage to go out there and spread the message, not only of just conservatism, but our faith as well," he said. "And so on this anniversary, I look back at not only what Charlie Kirk was able to accomplish, but the things that even in his passing he's still able to do."

On this day last year, Kirk, 31, was speaking at Turning Point's "American Comeback Tour" event at the Utah Valley University (UVU) in Orem, Utah, just after noon, when he was shot in the neck. He was pronounced dead at a local hospital shortly thereafter.

The suspect in the killing, then-22-year-old Tyler Robinson, is accused of firing one shot from a rooftop overlooking the quad where Kirk was speaking. A shocked crowd scattered as Kirk was rushed away from the scene.

Kirk, who was a father, left behind his wife Erika and two young children.

ERIKA KIRK REFLECTS ON FIRST YEAR OF GRIEF AFTER CHARLIE KIRK'S ASSASSINATION IN NYT ESSAY

"I think it's an extremely somber reminder of what we have in this country, that free speech is not free, that somebody died for that right, and Charlie Kirk [was] somebody who was brave enough to go out there on the college campuses and talk about conservatism and prove to the American people and the young generation that the conservative policies still work," Jones said.

Another Republican convention-goer, Mike Hurst of Mississippi, described what he remembers after first hearing the news that Kirk had been killed.

"It was one of the most gut-wrenching feelings I've ever seen, and of course, I went online, I saw the video, and to this day I'm still shocked that that could happen in our country," Hurst said, adding that we need more people like Kirk who encourage civil dialogue instead of political violence.

ACCUSED CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSIN ALLEGEDLY CONFESSED IN TEXTS, APOLOGIZED AND DESCRIBED MOTIVE, AGENT TESTIFIES

Robinson allegedly fled the rooftop, ditched his rifle in a wooded area across the street from the UVU campus, and fled the scene. A statewide manhunt persisted until the following night at around 10 p.m. when Robinson surrendered to authorities in St. George, Utah, about four hours south of the UVU campus.

His parents reportedly convinced him to turn himself in.

Pre-trial proceedings in Robinson's case are ongoing after a protracted battle regarding media access to the courtroom, and motions attempting to remove the death penalty as a possible sentence should Robinson be convicted.

Alex Stone of Missouri said young people are looking for a leader to fill Kirk's shoes, though his memory remains.

"Since Charlie's assassination, people have been lost," he said. "People have been looking for a voice or a leader to lead them in the right direction, and so we need people who are going to stand up and rise up and say, 'this is what is good, this is what is true, this what is beautiful.' And 'this is wrong, and here's what we should do in the face of it.'"

item.title: Hollywood Marine veteran Rob Riggle doubts modern stars would make Jimmy Stewart's WWII sacrifice
item.description: Marine veteran Rob Riggle doubts today's Hollywood stars would leave fame to serve like WWII bomber pilot Jimmy Stewart, who enlisted after winning an Academy Award.
item.content:encoded:
Hollywood Marine veteran Rob Riggle has doubts about whether today's stars would be willing to step away from the spotlight to serve in uniform like WWII bomber pilot Jimmy Stewart.

Stewart famously walked away from an Oscar-winning career at its peak to enlist in the U.S. Army Air Corps as a private, nine months before the attack on Pearl Harbor.

In the upcoming biopic "Jimmy," Riggle, who is a retired U.S. Marine officer, plays Colonel Terrill, Stewart's squadron commander and mentor.

TOM HANKS PUT 'BAND OF BROTHERS' STARS IN THEIR PLACE DURING BOOT CAMP 'MUTINY', NEAL MCDONOUGH REVEALS

During a recent interview with Fox News Digital, the 56-year-old actor and comedian weighed in on whether modern celebrities would be willing to make the same wartime sacrifice as the late movie icon.

"I would be surprised if anybody made that same choice today, especially an actor of his status," Riggle said.

"You got to remember, he won an Academy Award before the war," "The Hangover" star continued. "It wasn't like he was an up-and-coming actor. He was an established Academy Award-winning actor before the war. And then decided to put on the uniform and not in a safe way."

"He wanted to put on the uniform and serve where he could be used best," Riggle added. "And he was a pilot, so he put his hand in the air and went into harm's way. And I don't know if you'd see that today. I mean, I hope you would, but I would be surprised."

Stewart joined the military in March 1941, just 28 days after winning the best actor Academy Award for his performance in the classic 1940 film, "The Philadelphia Story." He had tried to enlist in late 1940 prior to winning his Oscar, but was initially rejected for being 5 pounds under the weight requirement for his 6'3 frame. Determined to serve, Stewart actively gained the weight so he could reapply and enlist right after the Academy Awards.

Due to his fame, the military initially tried to keep Stewart, who was a licensed commercial pilot, stateside as a flight instructor and used him for publicity and March of Dimes promotional tours. However, Stewart repeatedly requested overseas combat duty, appealing to his superiors to let him fly rather than serve in public relations.

99-YEAR-OLD WWII VETERAN AWARDED PURPLE HEART AFTER WAITING MORE THAN 80 YEARS

Stewart's persistence eventually paid off, and he was sent to England in late 1943 with the 445th Bombardment Group. He went on to fly 20 official combat missions over Nazi-occupied Europe as a command pilot, squadron commander, and wing commander in B-24 Liberator heavy bombers.

By the end of WWII in 1945, Stewart had risen from private to full colonel. His combat awards included the Distinguished Flying Cross, the Air Medal and the French Croix de Guerre.

REMEMBERING THE COLLEAGUES WE LOST: A VETERAN'S MEMORIAL DAY REFLECTION

Riggle noted that people may be unaware of the danger that Stewart willingly placed himself in while serving his country.

"I think Jimmy went through a lot harder service than most with the flying over Germany, dropping bombs, having to make those sorties under tremendous stress and loss of his peers," Riggle said.

"But I do think when you decide to serve your country, you're kind of writing a blank check with your life and limb and I think it takes a lot to do that, so I'm so proud of the way he served his country and came back and then found a way out of the darkness of PTSD," he added. "That was pretty amazing."

As a commander, Stewart carried the immense burden of sending young men into brutal anti-aircraft fire and Luftwaffe attacks. During his service, Stewart witnessed heavy losses among his men and carried deep guilt over the lives lost under his command.

Biographers and historians have documented that Stewart suffered from severe psychological trauma, which caused digestive issues, insomnia, nightmares, shakes and sweats. Though Stewart's symptoms indicated that he was experiencing Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder, the formal clinical diagnosis of PTSD was not established until 1980.

After returning to Hollywood, Stewart channeled his suppressed trauma into his post-war acting roles including his performance in 1946's "It's A Wonderful Life," in which he played George Bailey, a banker who was experiencing a mental breakdown, raging at his family, and contemplating suicide.

GARY SINISE SAYS HIS MONEY WOULD BE ‘MOVING A LOT FASTER OUT THE DOOR’ IF HE STILL LIVED IN CALIFORNIA

According to historians, portraying darker, more complex characters than in his pre-war Hollywood years enabled Stewart to process his trauma.

In the years following the war, Stewart enjoyed a successful career, built a family and continued his service in the Air Force Reserve for another two decades. Stewart died from a heart attack in 1997 at the age of 89.

While speaking with Fox News Digital, Riggle explained that he drew upon his own military experience in U.S. Marine Corp while portraying Colonel Terrill. Riggle served in the Marines for 23 years, reaching the rank of lieutenant colonel and serving deployments in Af­ghanistan, Albania, Liberia and Kosovo before retiring in 2013.

The actor noted that his service gave a personal understanding of what it means to send young men into harm's way.

"I myself was a Lieutenant Colonel so I know what it is to be in charge of a group of people," he said. "I was a Marine but I know what it's like to be responsible and in charge and I know the weight of leadership. So I felt for all the characters in the movie that have that responsibility of leading men and making decisions that could affect their lives or end their lives."

Riggle launched his comedy and acting career in 1997 in New York City while he was still serving on active duty in the Marines. He had a short stint as a cast member on "Saturday Night Live" from 2004 to 2005, and later made his breakthrough as a correspondent for "The Daily Show."

The actor later appeared in numerous sitcoms, including "New Girl," "Arrested Development," "The Office" and "Modern Family," in which he played Ty Burrell's character, Phil Dunphy's arch nemesis, Gil Thorpe.

He has also had roles in hit movies including "The Hangover," "Step Brothers," "The Other Guys," "Dumb and Dumber To" and "Let's Be Cops."

Riggle told Fox News Digital that serving in the Marines gave him the qualities and mindset that he needed to succeed in Hollywood.

"Tenacity, don't quit, never give up, get up and try again," he said. "All those intangible lessons of mental toughness and fortitude, you need to have those if you're gonna be in Hollywood or any life in the arts, really."

"Because people are going to reject you, people are gonna deny you, people are not gonna see it the way you see it," Riggle continued. "You've got to be able to take the blows and keep going forward. And I think that's what the Marines gave me with those intangibles."

Riggle also said that his military background has helped keep fame and Hollywood success in perspective.

"When you're a Marine, Uncle Sam doesn't care who you are," he said. "He still expects you to go do your job and every day get up and do it."

"I think it's great," Riggle added. "I think that it's very humbling and it's a good reminder. Get up and go do your job."

Riggle shared that he considers his military service to be among his top life achievements.

"It's got to be right up there in the top three, next to my kids," he said.

"There should be some mention of it on my tombstone, let me put it that way," Riggle added with a laugh.

Riggle noted that while Hollywood is generally appreciative of former service members, he believes many civilians still harbor a fundamental misunderstanding about why men and women choose to enlist in the first place.

"I have felt that Hollywood is actually very respectful toward its veterans," Riggle said. "It's been really nice to see. But if there are misconceptions out there, I think some people, again, this is a general statement, but I think people might think that people who join the military, they do it because they don't have any other choices."

"And that's simply not true," he continued. "They've got a tremendous amount of choices. And they choose to serve their country."

"It's an all-volunteer force," he added. "No one's making them do anything. So the people that put their hand in the air have made that decision in their mind and that decision is to serve something bigger than themselves. And I think it's quite honorable."

Directed by Aaron Burns and starring "Riverdale" alum KJ Apa as Stewart, "Jimmy" follows the actor's transformative journey from Hollywood stardom to World War II combat pilot. The movie also explores his return home as a decorated Colonel who is quietly struggling with PTSD, which was then known as "combat fatigue."

"Jimmy" depicts how Stewart was disillusioned and considering quitting acting when director Frank Capra (Max Casella) persuaded him to star as George Bailey in "It's a Wonderful Life" and how playing the role in the holiday classic enabled the actor to heal and reclaim his life.

Riggle told Fox News Digital that he was drawn to the project because it's a "great American story."

"I think it's a patriotic story," Riggle said. "I think people know Jimmy, especially younger generations, know him from his acting. I really wanted people — or I'm glad to be part of the story that's being told, about his service to his country."

"I hold it to high esteem,"he continued. "So I thought his journey was fantastic, it was amazing, and it was a true American journey."

"I think he's a hero," Riggle added.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Riggle expressed his hope that audiences who watch "Jimmy" and may be unfamiliar with his military service may come to see him in a new light.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"I hope they remember the man, Jimmy Stewart," Riggle said. "Most people just remember him from 'It's a Wonderful Life.' Every Christmas they see him and they're like, ‘Oh yeah, I love this movie.’ And there's so much more to the man."

"And I hope they remember that there are people out there — we see so much news about the bad guys," he continued. "There's a lot more stories of good guys, you're just probably not seeing enough of them. And this is a story about a really great guy who did what he thought was right, followed his heart, followed his conscience, and did what he thought he needed to do, and we're all better for it."

item.title: Democratic socialist backed by Bernie Sanders ousts Providence, Rhode Island mayor
item.description: Rhode Island Rep. David Morales, 27, defeated Providence Mayor Brett Smiley by 8 points after campaigning on rent stabilization and housing justice.
item.content:encoded:
Rhode Island State Rep. David Morales, a 27-year-old democratic socialist endorsed by Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., defeated Providence Mayor Brett Smiley in the Democratic primary Wednesday night, ousting the incumbent after one term.

If Morales wins the general election, he will be Providence's youngest mayor in history.

"Few believed that a 27-year-old democratic socialist could ever, few believed that we could ever take on big money, corporate real estate interests and endless attack ads – and we took them on and we won," Morales said in his victory speech, delivered partly in Spanish, after winning by roughly 8 points (54%-46%).

Smiley, 47, who faced his heaviest media scrutiny over his handling of the Brown University shooting last December, served just one term.

AMERICA’S QUIET SOCIALIST TAKEOVER IS SPREADING FROM TOWN HALLS TO CLASSROOMS

"So neighbors, with the bold agenda and the mandate that we have voted for, let's get ready. Providence, let's get ready."

Morales will face Republican nominee Dave Talan, 77, in November. Republicans hold no seats on the Providence City Council, and Democrats make up a majority of registered voters in the city. Former Vice President Kamala Harris beat President Donald Trump in the city by 51 points in 2024.

"The voters of Providence made their choice, and they chose David Morales as our next mayor in the Democratic primary," Smiley said in his concession speech after calling Morales. "While I’m not happy with that outcome, I’m so happy and proud of the campaign that we ran."

STATE OF PLAY: WHAT TO KNOW ABOUT POTENTIAL SOCIALIST SHOWDOWN BETWEEN TRUMP AND DC MAYOR AS VOTES POUR IN

Morales, who also received backing from Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., former Providence Mayor Jorge Elorza and several labor unions, campaigned on a progressive platform that included capping rent hikes, expanding affordable housing and raising taxes on polluters and corporate landlords.

"Nearly a year ago today, we launched a campaign centered around a simple vision that the working people who make Providence home deserve to live here," Morales said. "A simple vision that our neighbors deserve a mayor who will fight for them."

The contest was part of a broader series of Democratic primary battles between progressive challengers and more established incumbents. Morales sought to tap into frustration over housing costs and the direction of city government, while Smiley argued that his experience and record made him the better choice to lead Providence.

SOCIALIST INSURGENTS FORCE MODERATE DEMOCRATS INTO HIGH-RISK SHOWDOWN OVER MUST-HOLD RACES

"The same way that we campaigned, we are going to govern — in coalition, side by side with our neighbors," Morales said.

The primary also featured a battle over rent stabilization. The Providence City Council approved a measure that would have capped annual rent increases at 4% for certain apartments, but Smiley vetoed it in April. The council fell one vote short of overriding the veto in May.

MAMDANI’S AFFORDABILITY REVOLUTION STUMBLED AS RENT COSTS SOAR TO RECORD HIGHS

"When working people are getting priced out of the city that they love, then we must cap rent increases at 4% every single year," Morales said.

"We put housing justice on the ballot."

Morales also ran as a hard-liner on Providence being a sanctuary for illegal migrants, and against the Trump administration's effort to enforce U.S. immigration law.

"The city of Providence must use every tool that we have at our disposal to defend our immigrant community and protect us from the fascist ICE agents," Morales, the son of a Mexican immigrant mother, said.

item.title: Floating solar panels could save cities millions. Is your town next?
item.description: Lima, Ohio, has installed 3,120 floating solar panels on its Twin Lakes Reservoir, projecting nearly $10 million in electricity cost savings.
item.content:encoded:
What if your town could build a solar farm without giving up acres of valuable land? Lima, Ohio, is trying something different. The city has completed a 2-megawatt solar array that floats on the Twin Lakes Reservoir, its primary drinking water source.

More than 3,000 solar panels now sit on the water and feed electricity to the nearby water treatment plant. The city projects the system will save nearly $10 million in electricity costs over its lifetime. That kind of savings could get the attention of cities far beyond Ohio.

So, could floating solar panels eventually show up on a reservoir near you? Here's how the technology works, why cities are interested and what it could mean for your community.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.

Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com

WHO PAYS FOR US POWER BOOM? BLUE, RED STATES OFFER STARKLY DIFFERENT WAYS TO LOWER UTILITY BILLS AMID AI SURGE

Lima officially celebrated the completion of its Twin Lakes Floating Solar Project on Aug. 12. The final system includes 3,120 solar panels spread across about 3.6 acres of water, according to developer D3Energy. The 2-megawatt array sits on Lima's primary drinking water reservoir. That reservoir serves roughly 35,000 residents.

Next door, the city's water treatment plant processes about 14 million gallons of water each day. It also consumes more electricity than any other city facility. That makes the plant an obvious place to look for energy savings. Lima projects the floating solar system will save nearly $10 million in electricity costs over its lifetime. Earlier city estimates put first-year savings at roughly $200,000. For a city utility, that is serious money. Actual lifetime savings will depend on factors including future electricity prices and how the system performs over time.

Instead of attaching panels to racks planted in the ground, engineers mount them on floating platforms. Anchors and mooring lines keep the array in position.

Lima uses Ciel & Terre's Hydrelio floating system. Its anchoring setup connects to the banks and reservoir bottom. The design also allows the array to move as water levels change. The project uses bifacial solar panels, which can capture light on both sides.

Electricity travels from the array to eight inverters onshore. From there, the electricity helps power the water treatment plant. The result looks a bit like a traditional solar farm that traded grass for water.

Here is where the idea gets particularly interesting. Land costs money. It also competes with housing, businesses, agriculture and other development. Reservoirs already occupy space. Lima's floating array covers about four acres.

A land-based system producing the same amount of electricity would reportedly need at least 10 acres. That could make floating solar attractive to cities with limited open space. The panels can also sit near the facilities that need the electricity. In Lima, the water treatment plant sits right beside the reservoir. That reduces the need to find a distant solar site and then figure out how to move the electricity where the city needs it.

Researchers have also studied whether floating solar can help reduce evaporation by shading portions of the water surface. Of course, every reservoir comes with different conditions. Water depth, changing levels and recreational use can affect whether a project makes sense. Federal researchers also consider existing dam operations when evaluating potential sites.

LAWMAKERS TARGET ENERGY AFFORDABILITY THROUGH SWEEPING PERMITTING OVERHAUL IN NEW HOUSE BILL

This was one of my first questions. These panels are floating on the same reservoir that provides drinking water to about 35,000 people. Lima's system uses Ciel & Terre Hydrelio floats made from high-density polyethylene, or HDPE.

Ciel & Terre says its floating system complies with the BS 6920:2000 standard for nonmetallic materials that come into contact with water intended for human consumption. Still, communities considering floating solar have more to evaluate than whether the structure can float safely.

The National Renewable Energy Laboratory has examined environmental and regulatory questions surrounding floating solar. Its research notes that projects can affect water bodies differently depending on the location. That means a system that works well on one reservoir may require a different design somewhere else.

There is another number worth paying attention to. The Lima project cost about $5.3 million. Federal support played a substantial role in making the numbers work. The city received a $2.4 million Department of Energy grant. Combined with almost $900,000 in federal direct-pay tax credits, that support helped offset roughly half of the project's cost.

Those incentives covered a significant share of the upfront expense. That context is important when another city looks at Lima's projected $10 million in savings. A town considering floating solar would need to look at construction costs, financing and expected electricity production. Available incentives could change the calculation as well.

Lima began considering the project years before crews put panels on the water. City Council approved moving forward with the project in 2023. Construction began in 2025 before the system came online this August.

Lima may look unusual today, but floating solar has substantial room to grow. Ohio already has more than one project. D3Energy and ARP Solar completed a 1.5-megawatt floating array for Del-Co Water in Delaware, Ohio, in 2024. A 6-megawatt system in Monroeville is expected to come online before the end of 2026.

The bigger opportunity stretches far beyond Ohio. National Renewable Energy Laboratory researchers studied federally owned or regulated reservoirs across the U.S. They estimated those reservoirs have technical potential for 861 to 1,042 gigawatts of floating solar capacity.

That figure represents technical potential rather than a prediction that thousands of reservoirs will soon disappear under solar panels. Plenty of locations would never make sense.

Still, the scale helps explain why energy developers and local governments are taking a closer look at water. CyberGuy has covered this idea before on a much larger scale. India's Omkareshwar project showed how enormous floating solar installations can become. We have also seen developers rethink the shape of solar installations on land. One Texas company is building vertical solar towers designed to produce more power from a smaller footprint.

AMERICA’S BROKEN PERMITTING SYSTEM IS QUIETLY RAISING YOUR COST OF LIVING

Here is the part I would keep an eye on. Lima expects to save nearly $10 million in electricity costs over the project's lifetime. But that does not mean residents will suddenly see a cheaper water bill. The city could use those savings in different ways. Lower energy costs could help cover other expenses, pay for infrastructure upgrades or ease pressure on future rate increases.

So, if a floating solar project comes to your town, there is one question worth asking: Will any of those savings eventually make their way back to you? That answer could determine how much this technology really helps the people paying the bills.

You probably do not spend much time thinking about how much electricity your local water plant consumes. Yet you ultimately help pay for that electricity through taxes, utility rates or both. Floating solar gives cities another way to attack that expense without buying a huge parcel of land.

It also raises questions you should ask before cheering on a project. How much will it cost? How much electricity will it realistically generate? What happens to the savings? You should also ask what testing and monitoring will protect the water supply. Those answers will tell you whether a floating solar project makes financial sense for your community.

What I like about Lima's floating solar project is how practical the idea feels. The city already owns the reservoir, and its water treatment plant right next door uses a huge amount of electricity. So instead of finding another piece of land for solar panels, Lima put them on the water. Then there is the projected $10 million in savings. That certainly gets my attention. I want to see whether those savings hold up over time and, more importantly, whether residents eventually benefit from them. Lima also gives other cities something real to look at. We are seeing communities experiment with new ways to generate and store energy, from floating solar to massive battery projects. And who knows? The next solar project in your town may end up floating right on the water.

Would you be comfortable with thousands of solar panels floating on your town's drinking water reservoir if officials said the project could save millions, or would you need to see more long-term evidence first? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com.

item.title: Drake Maye gets dragged through the mud by NFL fans after horrific game, troubling trend
item.description: Drake Maye threw three interceptions as the New England Patriots blew a 10-point lead to Drew Lock and the Seahawks in the NFL season opener.
item.content:encoded:
The more things change, the more they stay the same.

For Drake Maye, that's not a good thing.

The New England Patriots gave up a 10-point lead to Drew Lock and the Seattle Seahawks in Wednesday night's NFL opener, and their star quarterback was, once again, a problem.

A big one.

DRAKE MAYE'S TERRIBLE DECISION GIFTS SEAHAWKS OPENING NIGHT WIN AS PATRIOTS LEFT STUNNED TO START NFL SEASON

Maye, coming off a postseason in which he turned it over eight times in four games, threw three more interceptions Wednesday night, including one of the worst picks you'll ever see on what ended up being the final, back-breaking play of the night for New England.

Lordy. I've watched it a dozen times, and it gets worse each time I press play. Just brutal on so many levels.

Anyone watching the game could smell that one coming, by the way. Maye couldn't connect on a pass down the field all night long, with almost every completion coming at the line of scrimmage.

New England's gameplan was shockingly basic: force-feed Rhamondre Stevenson 18 times for 2.7 yards a carry, and then throw it to ... Rhamondre Stevenson ... in the flat for a gain of 3.

That was it.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

It's become a familiar sight for football fans, dating back to last season's suspect postseason run — after a regular season that was equally suspect given the Pats played one of the easiest schedules in the league.

It's Year 3 for Maye, and, clearly, fans are starting to notice a trend:

I could go on and on. NFL Twitter is a hellscape when you throw up an egg like that. It doesn't help that this was the season opener and fans had eight months of hot takes to get off their chests.

I get it. It's what makes this sport the best in the world. Boston fans love their quarterbacks. They've been begging Drake Maye to be a Tom Brady replacement for three years now. They'll defend him to their last breath.

But last night was completely indefensible.

Maye went 1 of 6 on throws 15+ yards down the field, with three interceptions. That's almost impossible to do as an NFL quarterback — especially one who fans argued should've beaten out Matt Stafford for MVP last season.

The Patriots could never get it going on offense. Maye brutally underthrew A.J. Brown on a flea-flicker in the second quarter — Brown would later get hurt — and the team somehow blew a 10-0 lead to DREW LOCK in the fourth quarter.

The internet was ready to pounce, and Maye served them up a fastball right over the middle.

Obviously, it's just one game. The first game of the season is always weird, by the way. Odd things will happen this weekend that you won't see for the rest of the year. Trust me.

But, unlike last season, the schedule doesn't get any easier for Maye and the Patriots. They get the Steelers, Jags and then Bills over the next three weeks.

Maye will probably be fine.

But this one is worth monitoring.

item.title: Amazon cargo pilot repeatedly warned aircraft was 'too fast' before deadly Miami crash, NTSB says
item.description: The National Transportation Safety Board says one pilot warned the other was "too fast" for nearly two minutes before the Amazon cargo plane crash.
item.content:encoded:
One of the pilots of the Amazon cargo plane that crashed in Miami last weekend, killing five people on the ground, repeatedly warned the other pilot the aircraft was "too fast" during the final approach and after touchdown, according to newly released information from the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB).

The pilots have been identified as Capt. Joseph Carroll, 55, and First Officer Jaime Felipe Silva Molina, 37, both of cargo airline 21 Air.

The NTSB did not identify which pilot was making the warnings or which pilot was receiving them as they approached Miami International Airport on Sunday.

The warnings continued for nearly two minutes, but the receiving pilot never gave "a consistent verbal response" to them, according to the NTSB's summary of the cockpit voice recorder.

AMAZON CARGO JET PILOT REPORTEDLY TOLD WIFE, 'MY CAREER IS OVER' SHORTLY AFTER DEADLY CRASH

Information from the flight data recorder shows the plane made an unstable approach in strong winds. After touchdown, the pilots briefly tried to take off again by advancing the throttles and releasing the brakes before abandoning the maneuver about four seconds later.

The cockpit voice recorder also captured a series of automated warnings, including repeated "sink rate" and "too low terrain" alerts, as the aircraft descended toward the runway.

FlightRadar24 data indicates the Amazon plane first touched down nearly 5,000 feet into the airport's 9,360-foot Runway 30, leaving it with less than half the remaining runway to stop.

VICTIMS IDENTIFIED IN FATAL AMAZON CARGO JET CRASH AT MIAMI AIRPORT

The plane touched down awkwardly before the pilots briefly attempted a go-around, then resumed braking, according to the NTSB. The Boeing 767 then barreled about 1,300 feet beyond the end of the runway and struck a van, killing the five people inside.

The five people killed in the van were part of a crew that cleaned planes at the airport, NTSB Chair Jennifer Homendy said Tuesday.

Five others were injured, including two who were in critical condition as of Tuesday. The pilots, who were injured as well, were treated and released before speaking with investigators on Wednesday, according to The Associated Press.

The full transcript of the cockpit conversation has not yet been released as the investigation continues.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Sharing the basketball was the theme of the night for Team USA as its 31 assists set a new all-time record in the FIBA World Cup. A total of five different players picked up at least three assists against Hungary.

The red, white, and blue topped their group in the early stages of the tournament, but did receive a scare from Italy in their final tune-up before elimination play started, staving off the Italians 55-53.

item.title: Presidential flip? GOP insider predicts Trump change of mind on key AI policy ahead of midterms
item.description: Trump ally Amy Kremer predicts President Donald Trump will shift on AI data centers after hearing from Americans on the midterm campaign trail.
item.content:encoded:
EXCLUSIVE: A GOP insider making the conservative case for regulating artificial intelligence development predicts President Donald Trump’s full-throated support for data center expansion will soon change after he hears from the American people on the midterm campaign trail.

In an interview with Fox News Digital, Amy Kremer, a close Trump ally, Republican National Committee member and founder of "Humans First," warned that the voice of the average American is being left out of the ongoing AI data center debate. She believes that is about to change as the president prepares to hit the campaign trail in support of Republicans ahead of the midterms this fall.

Right now, Kremer asserted that Trump is "only hearing one side of the story from big tech."

"He's getting ready to go out on the campaign trail, and I think he's going to hear more from the American people on the data center side of things. And I hope he does," she said, adding, "I know the president, and his heart, and he would not like the way the Americans are being treated."

MAGA BEGINS TO CRACK AS 2026 GOP ROSTER BACKS AWAY FROM TRUMP'S TECH VISION

Kremer was pivotal in founding the modern Tea Party movement and through the years established several pro-Trump political action committees, including the "Great America PAC," the first and largest grassroots organization founded in 2016 to support then-candidate Trump.

Now, she is the chairwoman of "Humans First," a political group calling for an "America First approach to AI" that it says would keep the U.S. ahead of China while protecting American families, communities and jobs.

She said that while Trump has made it clear that he wants America to lead on AI development, she believes that innovation and safety are "not mutually exclusive."

"I love the president. He has been an amazing president. I know he wants us to lead the world in technology and innovation, and I support him in that," she said, while noting, "There's this narrative out there that [with] innovation, you have to forego safety, and it's just not accurate. It's not true."

TEA PARTY FOUNDER LAUNCHES NATIONWIDE 'DATA CENTER REVOLT' AGAINST AI DATA CENTER EXPANSION

As the GOP gathers in Dallas for its first midterm convention, Humans First unveiled a new data center policy outline that it is urging the president and Republicans in Congress and state legislatures to adopt. The plan, obtained exclusively by Fox News Digital, calls for greater local control over data center development and rejects the use of eminent domain for land seizures.

The plan opposes federal and state "efforts to strip communities of that authority," including through a federal data center moratorium, which many opponents of AI development have called for. Instead, the plan calls for local communities to be given the ability to welcome or reject new data center developments through zoning and land-use processes.

Additionally, the plan rejects what it describes as "blank-check tax breaks" and subsidies and states that "any incentives must be transparent and tied to enforceable benefits for the community."

The plan calls for full transparency on data center development, stating that "before approval, communities deserve to know the project's end user, electricity demand, water use, land requirements, infrastructure costs, tax incentives, permanent jobs and environmental impacts."

It also calls for protection for ratepayers so that families and small businesses do not pay higher electric bills. Instead, it states that data centers should pay the full cost of the power generation, transmission, grid upgrades and infrastructure they require.

TRUMP SAYS GOVERNORS, MAYORS SHOULD WELCOME AI DATA CENTERS NATIONWIDE

Two other provisions address some of the most controversial aspects of AI data center development: local water usage and development on farmland, which the plan refers to as a "strategic American resource that should be protected."

The way Kremer put it? She posited that "there are more regulations on a hot dog that you buy on a street corner in New York City than there are on these big tech companies with this technology."

"We are not anti-AI, we're not anti-technology, and we're not anti-data centers," she explained. "What we are is we want the American people to have a seat at the table and a voice in this conversation."

"We can lead on innovation, we absolutely can," she said. "But that doesn't mean that it has to be on the backs of the American taxpayers."

item.title: Ancient cult discovered in region traveled by Apostle Paul before Christianity took hold
item.description: Nine ancient inscriptions from Akmoneia in Phrygia, in modern-day Turkey, reveal the first proof of a Demeter fertility cult in the region tied to Apostle Paul's journeys.
item.content:encoded:
Millennia-old inscriptions uncovered in a region tied to the Apostle Paul are shedding new light on how ancient people practiced religion nearly 2,000 years ago.

A recent study examined nine newly documented inscriptions discovered during a survey of Akmoneia, an ancient city in the historical region of Phrygia, in modern-day western Turkey.

Hüseyin Uzunoğlu, an associate professor at Akdeniz University in Turkey, and Münteha Dinç, an associate professor at Uşak University, are the co-authors of the study, published in the journal Gephyra.

ANCIENT BOOK OF REVELATION CITY GIVES UP STUNNING SECRET BURIED FOR 1,500 YEARS

Phrygia is mentioned in the New Testament. It's associated with the missionary journeys of the Apostle Paul, who traveled through the region and helped spread Christianity across the Roman world.

But the newly documented inscriptions — which date between the first and third centuries A.D. — highlight the religious traditions that already existed in the region.

Among the most significant was an inscription concerning a statue of Demeter Karpophoros, a goddess associated with fertility and harvests.

Uzunoğlu told Fox News Digital that while the cult was already well established elsewhere in Asia Minor, there had previously been no written proof of its presence in Phrygia.

ARCHAEOLOGISTS IN ISRAEL UNCOVER 1,700-YEAR-OLD ROMAN-ERA STATUES BURIED FACE DOWN

"But until this inscription — and a closely related one we published a couple of years ago — there was no epigraphic proof that the cult existed in Phrygia at all, even though Phrygia was a major agricultural region," he said.

"So this fills in a real gap on the map of ancient religious practice."

Another inscription revealed that a benefactor named Demades had commissioned a torch-bearing statue, likely helping to illuminate Akmoneia's colonnaded main street at night.

"This wasn't just civic piety in the abstract. It was one wealthy citizen literally lighting up his city," Uzunoğlu said. "Torch-bearing statues are known from only two other sites … so it's a nice addition to a very short list."

CONSTRUCTION WORKERS CLEARING OLD BOMBS UNEXPECTEDLY FIND 'IMPORTANT' ANCIENT SANCTUARY

A different inscription honored a woman named Mandana as the city's high priestess. Her husband, Priscus, set up the monument.

"There's good evidence … of women holding such positions independently," said Uzunoğlu.

"Mandana's inscription looks like one of those cases: The honor is hers, not a shared one."

RARE 1,200-YEAR-OLD CHRISTIAN CROSS FOUND IN FIELD BY METAL DETECTORIST

The inscriptions also offer glimpses into the personal lives of Akmoneia's inhabitants.

Uzunoğlu said one funerary altar suggests that a tomb owner prepared the monument for himself and his wife on the condition that she remain unmarried after his death.

Another funerary stone carries epitaphs for two men who were likely soldiers.

The epitaph says that one of the men "fell victim to lawless hands," or was murdered, according to Uzunoğlu.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"They were probably comrades-in-arms commemorated together — a rare and human glimpse of military friendship in the epigraphic record," he said.

Overall, Uzunoğlu said the importance of the research lies in what the inscriptions reveal together.

"It's less about one blockbuster find than about how each new stone incrementally sharpens the picture of how Akmoneians worshipped, honored each other and buried their dead," said Uzunoğlu.

While the inscriptions are not directly related to Christianity, they offer a window into the religious landscape of Phrygia, a region where the faith gained an early foothold, according to Douglas Estes, a scholar of early Christianity and professor at the New College of Florida.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Though Phrygia is associated with the missionary journeys of the Apostle Paul, Estes — who was not involved in the recently published research — cautioned that it is not known whether Paul traveled through Akmoneia itself.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"We don't have all the details of Christian missions [in] that area, but we do know that there was a lot of dialogue and a lot [of] missionary work in the region," he said.

Estes said archaeological evidence points to Christianity gaining followers among ordinary people in Phrygia well before Emperor Constantine came to power.

"And so it was not a top-down approach, but rather a bottom-up approach, where regular folks were embracing Christianity," he said.

item.title: Shawne Merriman says Rams' Aaron Donald-Myles Garrett combo is 'insane' for NFL offenses: 'Pick your poison'
item.description: Shawne Merriman said the Aaron Donald and Myles Garrett pairing on the Los Angeles Rams creates an impossible "pick-your-poison" nightmare for offenses.
item.content:encoded:
Whenever a new season begins in any sport, it’s usually the team that won the previous year’s championship that has the biggest target on their backs.

For the 2026 NFL season, it doesn’t seem to be the Seattle Seahawks, but rather the team they beat in the NFC Championship Game to reach the Super Bowl: the Los Angeles Rams.

Super teams are hard to come by when 53 men are stacked onto a roster, but the Rams have come pretty close entering the new campaign, with the reigning MVP Matthew Stafford leading the way on a high-powered offense, while LA revamped its defense with a pair of Defensive Players of the Year on the defense live.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

And one of them came out of retirement just to take another crack at winning another Super Bowl ring.

Aaron Donald, the 10-time Pro Bowl and eight-time First team All-Pro defensive tackle, officially ended his days outside football by rejoining the team he helped to win a Super Bowl in 2021. He joins Myles Garrett, the reigning Defensive Player of the Year and new single-season sack record holder, whom the Rams acquired in a blockbuster trade with the Cleveland Browns this offseason.

If the Rams weren’t scary enough when Stafford & Co. have the ball in their hands, this combo strikes fear into the eyes of their opponents just by being on the schedule each week.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

The expectations and potential of what this combo could do to offenses in 2026 has got football players, coaches and fans in a collective whirlwind. And one former NFL star linebacker thinks the hype couldn’t be more real.

"Just insane. I mean, it’s insane because every week will be a pick-your-poison situation," Shawne Merriman, All-Pro linebacker for the San Diego Chargers and Buffalo Bills, told OutKick in a recent interview. "Who do you want to focus on? Because the other one is going to make plays."

"Me being in my situation when I played, I knew I was going to get a lot of slide protection and chips off the edge and things like that. But you can’t do it to both sides. They have enough playmakers that, if you leave those guys one-on-one, it’s going to be damaging."

To Merriman’s point, offensive lines will have to choose who they wish to focus on when the ball is snapped. It’s nearly impossible to be able to pick up Garrett and Donald with 1-on-1 matchups at the line without getting beat and potentially blowing up the play.

There’s a reason the term "game wrecker" is used for certain players, and it’s been used time and time again for both Donald and Garrett throughout their respective careers.

For Garrett especially, Merriman thinks joining the Rams will unlock an extra gear fans might not believe they’d ever see.

"I want to add that people don’t understand, I give a lot of credit to our offense on my career because we were able to score so many points," he explained. "I mean, Phil [Rivers], L.T. [LaDainian Tomlinson], [Antonio] Gates, we knew we were putting up points every game. So, what happens is, you pin your ears back and go when the score gets 14-3, or 17-6. You can pin your ears back and go as a pass rusher.

"Well, Myles Garrett, he never had that situation in Cleveland. He never had it with these guys in a decisive win, or teams had to throw the ball a lot because obviously you don’t want to throw the ball as much when Myles Garrett is sitting on the side. So, that’s the scary part. Now, he can just go because those games can get out of hand."

As for Donald, Merriman was very confident in saying that he is "still a top three player at 80% of what he is," which is what many have been echoing. As a defensive tackle, Donald was able to do things nobody at the position did on a consistent basis: get to the quarterback. He led the league in sacks in 2018 with 20.5, while totaling 111 over his future Hall of Fame career.

REIGNING MVP MATTHEW STAFFORD LOCKS IN EXTENSION WITH RAMS WORTH UP TO $60M WITH INCENTIVES

He may have set that Hall of Fame clock back a few years by returning, but at 35 years old, Donald is still one of the craftiest, strongest, and elusive defensive tackles the NFL has ever seen. Merriman expects him to prove why he’s one of the greats in 2026.

"If he comes back and he’s the same player – I’m sure it’s going to take some time to get used to football movements and get going again. But Aaron Donald is still a top three player at 80% in the NFL, which is scary," he said.

"You can’t comprehend what that looks like. We haven’t seen anything like this before, because Myles Garrett in his own right can go down as the best pass rusher of all time, at least at the defensive end position. I love Bruce Smith, he’s one of my favorite players. I wore No. 56 because of Lawrence Taylor, but before this thing is all said and done, [Garrett] can go down as the best on his own. And you gotta put Aaron Donald down as the one or two best D-tackles of all time."

Of course, all of this is being said before the Rams even kick off in Melbourne tonight at 8:35 p.m. ET, where Donald won’t be playing with L.A. wanting to give him more time to ramp up before taking the field once again. But the Rams are pegged as a team that embodies the "Super Bowl or bust" mantra this season.

If they don’t make it there, what will the conversation be? Is it one of the biggest failures by a franchise in NFL history?

"Football is a finnicky sport, man. There’s been some ‘super teams’ in the past where it’s big names on paper and things just don’t go their way," Merriman said. "But how they’re built and constructed, on both sides of the football by the way, it’s hard not to believe they end up, at the bare minimum, back in the NFC Championship Game this year."

item.title: How Charlie Kirk’s assassination changed the way conservatives approach hostile opponents
item.description: One year after Charlie Kirk's assassination, Turning Point USA allies weigh how to balance personal safety with showing up on college campuses.
item.content:encoded:
Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk built his public persona around confronting political opponents face-to-face, often in settings where disagreement and hostility were expected.

Now, one year after his assassination, conservative media personalities and influencers are still wrestling with how to keep themselves safe while also sparking conversations with the other side. Some say Kirk's death has made them more cautious about security, while others feel more determined to keep showing up despite the danger.

INSIDE CHARLIE KIRK’S EFFORT TO DEVELOP THE NEXT GENERATION OF CONSERVATIVE VOICES

For TPUSA reporter Savanah Hernandez, the answer is both, as she strives to cover important stories while also keeping herself safe.

"I do feel myself, as a woman, I was awarded a little bit more ability to go and cover various events or talk to certain people without the threat of violence. But after Charlie's assassination, all of that changed," Hernandez told Fox News Digital.

Hernandez recalled that during one of the first events she covered after Kirk's assassination, which was a protest outside a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facility, someone realized she was with TPUSA and proceeded to "light a MAGA hat on fire" and put it in front of her face. Months later, in April 2026, Hernandez was physically assaulted while reporting outside an ICE facility in Minnesota.

"As a journalist, I always want to get the story. I always want to get the shot. I always wanted to show my audience exactly what's going on, but, unfortunately, the reality of potentially dying on the street is something that I am very well aware of, as are all of my friends," Hernandez told Fox News Digital.

Daily Wire co-founder and host of "The Ben Shapiro Show" Ben Shapiro told Fox News Digital that while he has had round-the-clock security for years, Kirk's assassination changed how he approaches certain events.

"What I did say in the aftermath is I would never again do an outdoor event. Outdoor events are inherently riskier, very, very difficult to secure," Shapiro told Fox News Digital.

Shapiro said that while his team takes precautions to secure events, such as requiring tickets and using metal detectors, he knows that "you can't bring the risk all the way down to zero."

ERIKA KIRK URGES CONSERVATIVE STUDENTS NOT TO BACK DOWN IN FIRST SCHOOL YEAR SINCE CHARLIE'S ASSASSINATION

Michael Knowles, host of "The Michael Knowles Show," warned of "two opposite errors" that some could make in the wake of Kirk's assassination. The first, he told Fox News Digital, is to "take security so seriously that you never do anything," thus handing your opponents a victory "because they've shut you up." The second, is to "not take security seriously at all, in which case the left can shut you up by killing you."

"I think what Charlie endeavored to do and what we all endeavor to do is to have a prudent middle ground where we take the security seriously, but we don't allow the left to intimidate us into shutting up," Knowles told Fox News Digital.

Knowles recalled that he was set to appear alongside Kirk at an event slated to take place at the University of Minnesota 12 days after the TPUSA founder's assassination. In fact, the last message he received from Kirk was about the event.

"I remember thinking that morning, 'oh shoot, I owe Charlie a text, ah well, I'll get to it later,' and then he was killed," Knowles said.

Shortly after Kirk’s assassination, Knowles said he was asked whether he still planned to attend the event in Minnesota. He told TPUSA that the decision was ultimately up to the organization, and organizers ultimately decided the event should proceed.

"They said, ‘We think you should do it,’ which of course was the right answer," Knowles said.

Knowles told Fox News Digital that he views the decision as being consistent with Kirk's values. He said that while he was reluctant to speak for the late TPUSA founder, he believed that Kirk would have wanted conservatives to continue to "show up, bring a message of conservatism, a message of Christianity and everything in between to college campuses. I'm quite certain he would say that's the right thing to do."

Hernandez echoed a similar sentiment, saying that Kirk's assassination made her more determined to continue reporting from the ground.

"Despite the uptick in violence and the increased threats that everybody at Turning Point USA has been experiencing after his assassination, I think we're more emboldened than ever to continue to stay on the ground because Charlie's entire thing was about having conversations with people to reach out to the other side," she said.

Shapiro told Fox News Digital that, beyond security concerns, Kirk's assassination also underscored the broader problem with how political debates take place in the age of social media.

"I think that the entire value of debate may have declined just as a facet of social media, because so much of debate is not really about free exchange of ideas anymore. Now it's much more about the 15-second dunk," Shapiro said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Shapiro added that social media-driven viral clips of debates have incentivized public figures to provoke opponents, rather than engage with them.

"As the attention span decreases… you can score a point simply by getting up in front of a microphone and saying something egregious to somebody else," he said.

Shapiro warned that increasingly heated rhetoric had led to what he called "permission structures for violence," which he said "have become commonplace in American public life."

Knowles said he came to a sweeping conclusion following Kirk's assassination that differed from many in the conservative world. While some saw it as a moment to "double and triple down" on debating anyone, anywhere, Knowles said he drew the opposite lesson.

"My lesson that I drew was that no one debated ideas in the open marketplace with anyone with greater graciousness and openness than Charlie Kirk. And they murdered him for it," Knowles told Fox News Digital, adding that "we need to properly regulate the marketplace."

One year after Kirk's assassination, the microphones remain on, and campus events continue, but those who participate in them have a different understanding of what's at stake. Still, many show up to voice their opinions, even when they face opposition.

item.title: Charlie Kirk statue bound for NY's Times Square as sculptor defies threats ahead of unveiling
item.description: Sergio Furnari's $100,000 bronze Charlie Kirk memorial will be unveiled in Times Square on the one-year anniversary of the assassination Thursday afternoon.
item.content:encoded:
An Italian-born sculpture artist is set to unveil a six-figure tribute to Charlie Kirk in the heart of New York City this week — a move that he hopes will spark dialogue rather than division.

Sergio Furnari was still in bed when his daughter came home with the news that Kirk had been assassinated at a Turning Point USA event at Utah Valley University on Sept. 10, 2025.

"It took me a couple of seconds to connect," Furnari told Fox News Digital. "And then I kind of was, I would say, saddened by it."

ERIKA KIRK REFLECTS ON FIRST YEAR OF GRIEF AFTER CHARLIE KIRK'S ASSASSINATION IN NYT ESSAY

Within weeks, Furnari — who gained attention for his 40-foot sculpture of athlete Cristiano Ronaldo — was fielding calls suggesting he create a tribute to Kirk.

"I was like, ‘No way, I cannot get involved with politics,’" Furnari said. "But I [saw] how Erika [Kirk] got treated, including the parents of Charlie, and that’s what I think became my catalyzer[sic]."

ERIKA KIRK COMFORTS A STRANGER IN TEARS DURING HEARING FOR HUSBAND'S ACCUSED ASSASSIN TYLER ROBINSON

"If you’re a parent, no matter if you were Democrat or Republican, you should have a little bit of empathy," he continued.

Furnari got to work on the memorial — a 6-foot,-5-inch sculpture painted bronze and funded by his own savings.

"I did the first one in early December," Furnari said. "It came out good, different than [the final] one, and without a microphone. For me, it was just to test my skills."

"From there on, I became more passionate about it — just because of the way everybody was making fun of him," he added. "I feel like they killed him once, and they kill him each time, over and over again."

A YEAR AFTER CHARLIE KIRK'S MURDER, SOME COMICS ARE CALLING OUT JOKES ABOUT HIS DEATH

Within five months, the statue of a seated Kirk holding his famous microphone and wearing a T-shirt with the word "FREEDOM" adorning the front was complete.

However, the tribute also came with a monumental cost of $100,000, which was paid for by Furnari out of his own pocket.

INDIANA FARM VOWS TO ‘ABSOLUTELY’ DO CHARLIE KIRK CORN MAZE AGAIN DESPITE WAVE OF BACKLASH

"If I include my time, [it was] probably more than $100,000," Furnari told Fox News Digital, adding, "It sounds like a number that is like, ‘Oh my God,’ because there are people that don’t know the value of art."

Furnari is still looking to recoup the cost of the project and has launched an online fundraiser to crowdfund support, with the promise that "donors of any kind will have their name engraved on the monument’s platform."

HE FLED COMMUNISM. NOW THIS CALIFORNIA MAYOR IS HONORING CHARLIE KIRK AND REFUSING TO BACK DOWN

Despite the eye-watering price tag, Furnari insists that he is not an avid supporter of Kirk.

"It’s not like I agree with him. There’s a lot of stuff I didn’t agree with," Furnari said. "But still, freedom of expression and, in my case, freedom of creation — there are no boundaries, no borders. That’s where we kind of stand together."

The statue of Kirk is set to be unveiled in New York City’s Times Square on Sept. 10 at 2:33 p.m. to mark the one-year anniversary — down to the minute — of the conservative activist’s assassination.

"There’s lots of New Yorkers, millions of New Yorkers, who love Charlie," Furnari told Fox News Digital. "So come on by."

'ARE YOU EFFING KIDDING ME?' CALIFORNIA RESIDENTS REACT TO STREET BEING RENAMED AFTER CHARLIE KIRK

The artist also revealed he has received countless hate-filled messages in response to the memorial, with some individuals even threatening to deface the statue at the unveiling and mocking the way in which Kirk was assassinated.

"I get thousands, probably hundreds of thousands of comments, like, ‘Where is the hole?’ or ‘I will make sure you will find his head in your bed,’" Furnari said, adding, "Nobody really scares me. And when they threaten my life, it’s like whatever."

Furnari insists that the message behind the statue is apolitical, and his hope is that the tribute to Kirk will inspire both tolerance and creativity in the wake of his death.

"It’s a monument definitely to Charlie, but it’s even a monument to freedom of speech," Furnari said, adding, "The idea is to spread dialogue. Pure, simple dialogue — just the way [Kirk] did."

Fox News Digital reached out to TPUSA for comment.

item.title: Let socialists rob from the rich 100% and you still won’t be able to pay the bills
item.description: Tax the rich sounds simple, but Cato Institute estimates show seizing all top 400 billionaires' wealth covers just 9% of the DSA's $71 trillion platform.
item.content:encoded:
"Tax the rich." It's one of the easiest political slogans in America.

Need more money for government programs? Tax the rich.

Want free college or groceries? Tax the rich.

Want universal healthcare, government-funded childcare, housing programs and expanded Social Security? Just make billionaires pay their "fair share."

There's only one problem. The math.

THE MEDICARE FOR ALL TRADE-OFFS SOCIALISTS AREN'T TALKING ABOUT, ACCORDING TO EXPERTS

The Cato Institute recently decided to run the numbers on nine major proposals associated with the Democratic Socialists of America's 2026 platform. Cato estimates those proposals could cost somewhere between $71 trillion and $212 trillion over the next decade.

Now, that's a gigantic range and an important caveat to know. This isn't a Congressional Budget Office score of one piece of legislation. Cato assembled estimates from multiple studies to illustrate the potential magnitude of these policies.

JONATHAN TURLEY: ABDUL EL-SAYED’S WEALTH-TAX FANTASY COULD WRECK THE MICHIGAN ECONOMY

But let's take the low number. $71 trillion. Surely America's billionaires can cover that, right?

Let's find out.

AOC DOUBLES DOWN ON ‘MYTH’ OF EARNING A BILLION DOLLARS, CLAIMS FORTUNES ARE BUILT ON ‘ABUSE’

Cato estimates America's 400 richest people collectively held approximately $6.6 trillion in wealth in 2025. So, let's do something even the most aggressive tax proposal doesn't suggest.

Take it all. Not 40%. Not 70%.

100%.

Sell the yachts. Sell the stocks. Sell the businesses. Empty the bank accounts.

TOP SENATE DEM’S NEW TAX IDEA GETS TORCHED AS CRITICS WARN NEARLY EVERY AMERICAN COULD PAY

Congratulations. You raised $6.6 trillion. Unfortunately, you've covered only about 9% of Cato's low-end estimate.

And there's another little problem. You can only confiscate someone's fortune once. Next year, you need another taxpayer.

SEN TOM COTTON: DEMOCRATS SAY SOCIALISM WILL HELP. HISTORY SAYS IT WILL HURT

Fine. Let's go after corporations. Cato estimates domestic corporations could generate approximately $35 trillion of after-federal-tax profits over the next decade. Let's take every additional dollar of that, too.

Forget shareholders. Forget reinvestment. Forget dividends. Take everything. Including your jobs. Even then, according to Cato's calculations, you'd cover only about half of its $71 trillion low-end estimate.

U.S. DEBT BLOWS PAST $40 TRILLION, JEOPARDIZING QUALITY OF LIFE FOR EVERY AMERICAN

And remember this. America already has bills.

The federal government is projected to run roughly $24 trillion in deficits over the coming decade under the baseline cited by Cato. We're already spending money we don't have before adding trillions in new promises.

Here's where the math gets even more interesting. Cato cites Joint Committee on Taxation economists who studied how much additional revenue could be generated by pushing top federal income-tax rates toward their revenue-maximizing level.

Their conclusion? Surprisingly little.

Cato calculates the additional revenue at roughly $400 billion over 10 years. Why? Because taxpayers aren't mannequins.

Change tax rates dramatically and people change behavior. They work differently, invest differently, realize income differently and find different legal ways to structure their finances.

That's why you can't simply take today's income and multiply it by whatever tax rate sounds good on television.

This is the part politicians don't like discussing. You can argue America should have higher taxes. You can argue government should provide more services. Those are legitimate political debates.

But let's stop pretending there's a magical vault somewhere containing enough billionaire money to pay for every promise Washington wants to make.

There isn't.

Eventually, the math works its way down the income ladder. First the billionaires. Then the millionaires. Then successful business owners. Then upper-middle-income families.

And eventually?

You. That’s right. Uncle DSA Sam wants you.

British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher famously said the problem with socialism is that eventually you run out of other people's money.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Forty years later, we can debate the politics.

But it's getting awfully difficult to debate the math.

item.content:encoded:
Those who were present at Ground Zero on Sept. 11, 2001, continue to experience the physical effects of their exposure.

As Lower Manhattan was engulfed in dust and debris from the remnants of both towers, first responders and survivors were forced to breathe in toxic air.

More than 400,000 people were exposed to toxic contaminants, physical-injury risks and stressful conditions in the days, weeks and months following the attacks, according to the World Trade Center Health Program.

SCIENTISTS DISCOVER POSSIBLE LINK BETWEEN 9/11 AND ACCELERATED AGING

As of March 2025, 8,215 people who had enrolled in the WTC Health Program had died, including 5,844 responders, as reported by the CDC. The figures include deaths from all causes; the program does not track whether a member’s death was related to 9/11 exposure.

In an interview with Fox News Digital, Mordechai Shedrowitzky, a volunteer EMT who responded on 9/11, shared how his exposure led to multiple hospitalizations and, ultimately, major surgery.

Queens-born Shedrowitzky, 51, was living in Brooklyn at the time of the attacks. After helping cover his local area for much of the day, he headed into Lower Manhattan that evening to assist with the response.

"My most vivid memory was actually entering Manhattan from Brooklyn," he said. "As we approached the tunnel, the first thing we noticed was there were no lights, there was no electricity in the area, it [was] pitch black."

FOX NEWS' ERIC SHAWN REVEALS CANCER AND RESPIRATORY ILLNESS FROM 9/11 TOXIC DUST

"When we entered the tunnel, there was a tremendous amount of swirling debris, at speeds that I just can't even imagine."

Once Shedrowitzky and his team arrived at South Street Seaport, where his ambulance was staged with others, he described the debris as "overwhelming."

"I remember the engine actually sputtering at times," he said. "I would imagine that it was taking in a tremendous amount of dust."

"We were definitely not cognizant of what effect ... the air might have on us. And therefore, we did spend a significant amount of time outside of the ambulances, just commiserating with the people around us."

Shedrowitzky said he "thought it was over" once he left the scene. But years later, he noticed small symptoms that were turning into a big problem.

His pre-existing asthma — which typically flared during seasonal changes and caused coughing that required an inhaler — was worsening each year.

AMERICA'S FIREFIGHTER SHORTAGE HITS CRISIS LEVEL AS EMERGENCY CALLS TRIPLE, PUTTING LIVES AT RISK

"I started to require oral steroids," he said. "I would have wheezing; I would have coughing. It would last longer; it would be more serious ... I wouldn't be able to go to work, wouldn’t be able to take care of my kids. So, the effects were definitely increasing over time."

Shedrowitzky added that his condition was "getting to the point where it was leading to frequent respiratory infections and hospitalizations."

"It took a number of years, many years, for us to realize that what was going on with my health was probably related to 9/11."

In 2019, Shedrowitzky described that his condition got "significantly worse," after experiencing a cough that wouldn’t resolve itself, even after the "highest doses" of steroids and antibiotics.

NAVY VETERANS REUNITE AFTER 30 YEARS FOR 'GRUELING' CROSS-COUNTRY BIKE CHALLENGE HONORING 9/11

Shedrowitzky ultimately was put in touch with the World Trade Center Health Program – a federal program administered by the CDC – where his condition was classified as 9/11-related and was monitored.

It was eventually confirmed that Shedrowitzky had tracheobronchomalacia, a condition in which the walls of the windpipe and major airways weaken and collapse during breathing.

"[It] was probably secondary to both the asthma getting worse as well as steroid use over the years to try to treat those symptoms," he said.

In 2024, Shedrowitzky underwent a procedure called a tracheobronchoplasty to structurally reinforce his trachea and main bronchi.

RUDY GIULIANI REVEALS HE HAD 'SPIRITUAL EXPERIENCE' WHILE IN PNEUMONIA-RELATED COMA

Two years after the procedure, he said he is feeling "much better," although he still experiences occasional infections. He hopes to return to work as a physical therapist soon.

"Even a couple of months ago, I wouldn't have been able to speak for more than a very short time," Shedrowitzky said.

As a father of six, Shedrowitzky – who is now also a grandfather of two – said his condition made it difficult for him to spend time with his children as they were growing up.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"Things as simple as lifting my children, even speaking to them," he said. "The amount of time that I spent in the hospital and its effect on them was quite significant."

"Now, they're older, but my ability to spend time, interact with them ... has been greatly improved."

Dr. Denise Harrison, medical director of the NYU Grossman School of Medicine WTC Health Program Clinical Center of Excellence, has been involved in post-9/11 healthcare since 2002.

The program has since grown to provide screening, monitoring and treatment for people experiencing health effects related to their 9/11 exposure.

The doctor noted that the dust on 9/11 was "highly alkaline," which can be "very irritating" to the airways.

"Usually, the larger size dust gets deposited in the upper airways and the smaller size dust gets deposited in the lower airways," she told Fox News Digital. "Because of the overwhelming nature of the disaster, a significant number of large particles got deposited into the lower airways as well. So, this is not just the airways, but also the digestive tract, in the esophagus."

Harrison said patients often report sinus problems, asthma and COPD. These conditions can occur alongside other "aerodigestive" issues, including gastroesophageal reflux disease, which may complicate diagnosis and treatment.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Other 9/11-related conditions may also be interlinked.

"We have patients with asthma and PTSD who might perceive their asthma symptoms differently than the patients without PTSD, so that requires a combination of providers," the doctor said.

Shedrowitzky urged other first responders who are experiencing health issues to not wait to get help and to confirm that what they’re experiencing may be linked to 9/11.

"Continue to be monitored so that potential issues can be picked up early," he advised.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"If we can look back and see the quality of life that it's robbing you of, it might push you to contact the World Trade Center Health Program, get the help that you need."

As of March 31, 2025, the WTC Health Program had more than 130,000 currently enrolled members.

The program, which is authorized through 2090, operates branches across multiple health systems, including NYU Langone Health, Mount Sinai, Northwell, Stony Brook and Rutgers.

Harrison reiterated that the health effects of 9/11 exposure remain "persistent," and can be exacerbated by the environment and other illnesses. Experts predict that the fallout will continue for decades to come.

"Symptoms are still ongoing and research is still ongoing," she said, urging the public and responders to "have patience."

"While it might not directly benefit them or may provide some benefits now, it could be more beneficial in the future and help the overall response to disasters."
