item.title: How 9/11 transformed synagogue security into a new reality for the Jewish community
item.description: FBI data shows Jews face 63% of religiously motivated hate crimes as communities prepare for Rosh Hashanah on Friday, Sept. 11 amid rising threats.
item.content:encoded:
At sundown on Friday, Sept. 11, as America marks 25 years since the terrorist attacks that killed nearly 3,000 people, Jewish families across the country will welcome in Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish new year marking 5787.

They will enter synagogues at the moment of peak annual attendance, walking past armed guards, security cameras, secured doors and bag checks.

The convergence brings into focus how the Sept. 11 attacks transformed security in American synagogues and helped create the national infrastructure that now protects Jewish life.

FOX NEWS MEDIA ANNOUNCES EXTENSIVE 9/11 ANNIVERSARY COVERAGE FROM GROUND ZERO, PENTAGON AND SHANKSVILLE

When Rosh Hashanah began six days after the attacks in 2001, a security guard stationed outside a synagogue was still unusual. Twenty-five years later, security is no longer an occasional precaution. It has become a permanent precondition of Jewish communal life.

"The confluence of events, the 25th anniversary of 9/11 and Rosh Hashanah, is really very meaningful to us," Eric Fingerhut, president and CEO of Jewish Federations of North America, told Fox News Digital. "If you trace the evolution of the security situation for the Jewish community in North America, you see that 9/11 really was a major turning point."

Before the attacks, Fingerhut said, synagogues may have relied on police to direct traffic during the High Holidays or installed basic alarm systems, but there was no widespread belief that Jewish communities needed protection from threats to their physical safety.

"That changed on 9/11," he said. "The Jewish community understood quite clearly that the people who attacked the World Trade Center and the Pentagon were attacking America that day, but they had a special animus for the Jewish community and the Jewish people."

Fingerhut said that shift led Jewish Federations of North America to help create the Secure Community Network after 9/11, giving communities a model for protecting Jewish institutions and a unified channel to federal law enforcement.

For generations, Rosh Hashanah preparation meant apples and honey, prayer books and the shofar. Now the checklist also includes secured entrances, emergency plans and congregants standing watch while their neighbors pray.

The price of that new reality is staggering.

MARYLAND SYNAGOGUE SUES COUNTY OVER LAW RESTRICTING CONCEALED CARRY NEAR HOUSES OF WORSHIP

A national study by Jewish Federations of North America found that Jewish communal institutions spend an estimated $1 billion annually on security. Based on an examination of more than 4,500 institutions, that amounts to nearly $2.8 million every day simply to keep Jewish life open and accessible.

The organization leads the national initiative placing professional security directors across all 141 Federation communities.

Rabbi Chaim Steinmetz, senior rabbi of Congregation Kehilath Jeshurun on Manhattan’s Upper East Side, described the contrast on his own block.

"If you walk past the churches on our block, the doors are wide open, inviting people in," Steinmetz told Fox News Digital. "But at our synagogue, there are security cameras, a double door system and a line of guards outside, at the cost of untold thousands of dollars."

That security is no longer reserved for major institutions or large cities. From New York and Florida to Michigan and Los Angeles, ordinary worshipers are training in situational awareness, access control, surveillance detection, emergency response and coordination with law enforcement.

The Community Security Service, or CSS, said more than 20,000 people completed its training in 2025. Of those, 6,100 volunteers protected 440 synagogues and nearly 100 Jewish events, logging more than 300,000 guard hours across 24 states.

The Secure Community Network (SCN) provides national intelligence and coordination. In 2025, it recorded 4,400 incident reports, trained 40,000 people and made 851 referrals to law enforcement.

"While the threat environment accelerates, our community has never been more prepared, informed or engaged," Michael Masters, SCN’s national director and CEO, told Fox News Digital. "This year our Duty Desk logged nearly 3,200 threat incidents, pacing ahead of last year."

Steinmetz said threats to the Jewish community "exploded after Oct. 7th," adding that "the hatred of Israel encourages antisemites to come out of the woodwork."

The FBI recorded 1,528 hate crime incidents targeting Jews in 2025, representing 63% of the nation’s 2,408 religiously motivated incidents. Jews comprise roughly 2% of the U.S. population, yet incidents targeting Jews represented 14% of all hate crimes reported nationwide.

ANTISEMITIC VIOLENCE ESCALATES AS DEADLY WEAPON ATTACKS SURGE IN 2025: REPORT

During the first eight months of 2026, major crime fell 6.2% across New York City, while confirmed hate crimes targeting Jews rose 8%, from 212 to 229, according to new NYPD figures. That averages nearly one such crime every 25 hours.

Fox News Digital contacted NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch about the department’s High Holiday preparations. The NYPD said it will hold a briefing ahead of the holidays and provide additional security details at that time.

In neighboring New Jersey, the state Office of Homeland Security and Preparedness (NJOHSP) said it is coordinating with the state Attorney General’s Office, New Jersey State Police, the FBI’s Newark field office, local law enforcement and community partners.

"Together, we are protecting houses of worship, helping ensure every New Jerseyan can practice their faith without fear, and keeping New Jersey safe and secure," NJOHSP said.

The coordination follows recent attacks on Jewish institutions.

On Aug. 14, a man was charged with allegedly disrupting a Friday night service attended by approximately 375 people at Manhattan’s Central Synagogue, damaging ceremonial candlesticks and assaulting a congregant and security guard. The charges against include federal hate crimes and damaging religious property resulting in bodily injury.

Five months earlier, an attacker inspired by Hezbollah rammed a pickup truck carrying gasoline and fireworks through the doors of Temple Israel in West Bloomfield, Michigan, according to the FBI. Armed with a rifle and hundreds of rounds, he struck one security guard and exchanged gunfire with others.

Inside were 140 children at the synagogue’s early childhood center. Every child and staff member escaped without physical injury and the guard survived.

For Steven Ingber, CEO of the Jewish Federation of Detroit, the assault remains a powerful reminder of the need for vigilance as families prepare to gather.

"We take the security of our community with the utmost seriousness, and, of course, the assault on Temple Israel remains fresh in our minds," Ingber said. "We will enter the High Holidays vigilant and prepared. But we will also enter them with confidence and pride."

Rabbi Aaron Starr of Congregation Shaarey Zedek in suburban Detroit, who also serves as president of the Michigan Board of Rabbis, said Jewish Michiganders are entering the new year "with a feeling of heaviness."

"From marking the 25th year since the terrorist attacks on 9/11 to marking six months since the terrorist attack on our community and especially our children, anxieties are heightened," Starr told Fox News Digital exclusively. "We enter with heaviness, but we are also filled with hope for a better tomorrow."

LOX & LOADED: JEWISH GUN GROUP PARTNERS WITH NRA AMID RISING ANTISEMITISM

"No family should have to weigh their safety against their faith," Fingerhut said.

Employing one full-time security guard costs an estimated $90,000 annually, according to Jewish Federations of North America. The organization is advocating for greater federal support through the bipartisan Jewish American Security Act, which would strengthen security assistance for at-risk nonprofit institutions.

For Jewish communities, the question is no longer whether security is necessary, but who will bear the growing cost of making worship possible.

SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER

Steinmetz called that cost "a vicious tax on the Jewish community," one "levied by the antisemites."

For Fingerhut, the purpose of security is not simply to prevent an attack. It is to ensure fear never determines whether a Jewish family participates in Jewish life.

"We do not want anyone to make the choice not to participate in Jewish life because they are afraid for their safety," Fingerhut said. "What we have learned is that the visible presence of security, and the real impact of that security, is what enables and encourages people to come out and participate in Jewish life."

Fingerhut’s message to Jewish communities in America and around the world was clear: do not retreat, but continue to "lean into Jewish life."

He said, "We will make sure that there is safety and security in place so that we can all feel confident in our involvement in Jewish life."

That is the purpose, according to the experts, of every guard, camera and volunteer: not to turn a synagogue into a fortress, but to ensure that Jewish life continues inside.

item.title: Calling Democrats ‘communists’ won’t win Gen Z — Republicans need a better offer
item.description: The first Republican midterm convention at the American Airlines Center has already brought real energy, but a Gen-Z conservative argues solutions must replace outrage.
item.content:encoded:
I’m sitting in the American Airlines Center as the first-ever Republican midterm convention gets underway in Dallas, and the energy is real. The room is loud. The crowd is locked in. People came here because they know November is not a drill.

That’s the good news.

The less comfortable news is this: just calling Democrats communists is not a strategy. Yes, they are. The agenda is collectivist. The instincts are coercive. The destination is bigger government, weaker families and a generation trained to look to the state for everything.

But their lies, empty promises and dangling "free" things in front of my generation are working. Emotions work. Subsidized housing talking points work. Student-debt theater works. Climate panic works. Identity sermons work. They do not need to be honest. They need to be first, loud, and simple.

I'M GEN Z: IF THE GOP WANTS MY VOTE, STOP THE SPEECHES AND FIX THE HOUSING CRISIS

If our answer is just "they’re communists," we lose the people who never took a political theory class and never will. They hear the word, shrug and go back to the pitch that sounds like relief.

We cannot keep crying about it from the sidelines. We have to offer something better, something that a 20-year-old like me can actually picture: work that pays, housing that is not a fantasy, energy that is cheap, schools that teach instead of lecture, streets that are safe and a government that stops treating ambition like a moral defect.

This convention is the first time I have heard some of that from our side in a concentrated way. Not just contrast. Not just diagnosis. Actual counteroffers — tax relief that hits paychecks, border enforcement that is measurable, energy abundance instead of rationing and candidates who talk about building things instead of merely condemning the other tribe.

REPUBLICANS HEAD TO DALLAS WITH ONE MISSION: DEFY HISTORY AND WIN BIG

That is the part that matters.

Name-calling is catharsis. Solutions are politics. Democrats have spent years selling feelings and subsidies. If Republicans spend the next eight weeks only selling outrage, we will walk into November with high energy and a losing argument.

REPUBLICANS CAN WIN THE MIDTERMS IF THEY JUST STOP UNDERSELLING SUCCESS

Dallas should be the start of something, not a two-night pep rally. I hope this is not the last time before the midterms that our side talks like people who intend to govern, not just people who intend to be right.

The other side is not winning because they are smarter. They are winning parts of my generation because they showed up with a story. We finally started answering with one. Don’t stop.

YOUNG CONSERVATIVES REVEAL WHAT’S TOP OF MIND AS GOP, DEMOCRATS BATTLE FOR 'HOPELESS' GEN Z VOTERS

The last year and a half gave us more than talking points. The no-tax-on-tips-and-overtime policy is showing up in real returns. Seniors got the promised Social Security tax relief. The Working Families Tax Cuts put money back in paychecks. The border is no longer a slogan: catch-and-release ended, interior releases went to zero for months, and the wall and agents finally got funded. Trump Accounts give kids a start on savings instead of debt mythology. Energy leasing came back. That is a record. Stop whispering it to donors and start saying it to 20-year-olds.

MILLIONS TAP TRUMP TAX CUTS THIS FILING SEASON AS REFUNDS TOP $3,400

After Dallas, President Trump should take this same arena energy on the road. Tour campuses. Pack college arenas the way this hall is filled. Do not wait for young voters to find a clip. Take our message to them. Put two slides behind him. First: promises kept, with checkmarks. Tips. Overtime. Senior relief. Tax cuts that hit filings. A closed border. Accounts for kids. American energy. Make them look at the list instead of a Democrat’s poster about "free."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Then put up the second slide: what Gen Z is still owed in the last two years of this term. Housing you can actually buy, not another voucher speech. Power bills that stop eating the paycheck. Trades and apprenticeships with the same dignity as a four-year degree. Colleges that compete on price and speech instead of ideology. First jobs that hire for work, not politics. Cities that feel safe enough to stay in. Ownership, not a new subscription to the state.

That is how you beat the other side’s offer. They sell cancellation, panic and belonging. We should sell keys, hours, watts and a wage. Dallas cannot be a two-night pep rally with a better diagnosis. Take the checkmarks on tour. Take the unfinished list with them. 

My generation has already heard the word communist. What we have not heard enough is a deal.

item.title: Former NHL player, coach and longtime ESPN analyst Barry Melrose dead at 70
item.description: Barry Melrose's wife confirmed his death at 70 to ESPN, two years after his Parkinson's disease diagnosis forced his retirement from broadcasting.
item.content:encoded:
Barry Melrose, the former player and coach who led the Los Angeles Kings to the 1993 Stanley Cup Final before becoming one of hockey’s most recognizable voices in broadcasting, has died. He was 70.

ESPN announced Melrose’s death Wednesday after his wife notified Steve Lacy, a former ESPN colleague. Melrose was diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease in 2023, prompting his retirement from the network. He joined ESPN in 1996 and spent nearly three decades with the network.

"For decades, Barry Melrose was one of the most distinctive and trusted voices in hockey," the network said in a statement. "His knowledge of the game was deep, his candor was refreshing, and his passion was unmistakable. He was a foundational part of ESPN's hockey coverage, and fans and teammates truly appreciated his entertaining delivery and charismatic personality."

BILL RASMUSSEN, ESPN FOUNDER WHO CONCEIVED A CABLE NETWORK DEVOTED TO SPORTS, DEAD AT 93

"We send our deepest condolences to his loved ones. He always kept it interesting and he will be missed."

Melrose stepped away from sports broadcasting in 2008 for a brief return to coaching, serving as head coach of the Tampa Bay Lightning for 16 games. Melrose compiled an 84-108-29 record as an NHL head coach.

Melrose had a relatable everyman’s broadcasting style, bringing a sense of humor to his insights, and was easily recognized by his goatee and slicked-backed hair.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"From the flowing locks of his distinctive mullet to the flared lapels of his trademark long suit coats, Barry Melrose cut an unmistakable figure whenever you were fortunate enough to run into him at a rink or catch him on your television screen," NHL Commissioner Gary Bettman said in a statement. "You were even more fortunate if you engaged him in conversation or listened to his analysis because he never failed to boost your love of the game of hockey."

"Barry was my best friend at ESPN," John Buccigross, a longtime colleague of Melrose’s at the network, wrote on social media Wednesday.

"A big brother figure of rock solid values. I am shook to my core. Barry gave his life to hockey and some of his ESPN family, like me, learned of his shocking death today while at a hockey rink in Las Vegas preparing for the upcoming season. Chilling and fitting -- the rink was Barry's home. A more beloved ESPN institution there has not been. We love you, Barry. Forever."

NEW DETAILS EMERGE SURROUNDING FOUR-TIME STANLEY CUP WINNER CLAUDE LEMIEUX'S DEATH

From rural Kelvington, Saskatchewan, Melrose began his professional hockey career with the Cincinnati Stingers of the now-defunct World Hockey Association in 1976. He played three seasons in Cincinnati, the final one alongside a young Mark Messier, before making the jump to the NHL with Winnipeg in 1979 after the WHA folded.

Melrose went on to play for Toronto and Detroit, where he closed his career following the 1985-86 season.

He finished with 10 goals and 33 points and 728 penalty minutes in 300 career NHL regular-season games, and he skated in seven more in the playoffs. His WHA totals were five goals and 32 points and 343 penalty minutes in 178 games with Cincinnati.

Melrose is survived by his wife, Cindy, and their two children.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Charlie Kirk assassination: New UVU president says it will continue to 'host the frays,' embrace free speech
item.description: UVU's new president revealed his two daughters were just yards from Charlie Kirk's assassination and vowed to continue fostering free speech on campus.
item.content:encoded:
PROVO, Utah — A year after Charlie Kirk was assassinated in the central courtyard at Utah Valley University, school officials will close campus for the day — as the school's new president revealed his own daughters were at the scene and vowed to continue to foster free speech in higher education.

Dr. Jon Anderson, who joined UVU just before the start of the fall 2026 semester, was in his prior role as president of Pennsylvania Western University when Kirk was shot and killed on Sept. 10, 2025, but his family has roots in Utah, he told Fox News Digital in a sitdown interview.

His wife called him to break the news, he said.

JUDGE IN ACCUSED ASSASSIN TYLER ROBINSON'S CASE EXPLAINS WHY DEATH PENALTY REMAINS ON TABLE IN WRITTEN ORDER

"I had two daughters and a son-in-law. They were about 10 yards from the assassination when it happened," he said. "And so I knew that our future would be tied to it in one way or the other."

"When the opportunity came up to come home — this is the place that I'm from — and help this institution move forward and heal, it's something I leaned into immediately," he told Fox News Digital. "I wanted to be here to help in any way that I could, and I have found since coming here, this place is so resilient. Its people are gritty, they're ready to move forward, and they're to learn from everything that we can learn from that day."

ERIKA KIRK REFLECTS ON FIRST YEAR OF GRIEF AFTER CHARLIE KIRK'S ASSASSINATION IN NYT ESSAY

With students, faculty and other campus staff dealing with Kirk's assassination in their own ways, Anderson said the campus will be closed on Sept. 10, the one-year mark.

"I think one thing all of us at UVU have learned is that traumatic events, sometimes there's an initial reaction and sometimes there is a delayed reaction, and it's important for us to be very empathetic with each other as everyone goes through the healing process in their own way," he added.

ERIKA KIRK URGES CONSERVATIVE STUDENTS NOT TO BACK DOWN IN FIRST SCHOOL YEAR SINCE CHARLIE'S ASSASSINATION

Although the school is not hosting an official event, he said Turning Point USA plans to hold its own memorial on campus.

"We want people to have their own space to heal in their own way," he said. "TPUSA is using some space on campus to hold their event here, and we are supportive and reflective of that."

HOW CHARLIE KIRK INSPIRED HIS MENTOR'S FIGHT TO DEFEND REALITY

Kirk was a founder of TPUSA and was speaking at an event sponsored by its UVU chapter at the heart of campus when he was killed. The group will hold its memorial at UVU's UCCU Center at 6:30 p.m. MT on Sept. 10.

As for plans for a potential permanent memorial, Anderson said work is underway from a group including board members and students.

"They're sorting through lots of voices, getting people to the table to talk through what that might look like, looking at other institutions, what they have done," he said. "I can't guarantee that it's going to be anytime soon, but I can tell you if and when that happens, it will be thoughtfully done and well placed."

INSIDE CHARLIE KIRK’S EFFORT TO DEVELOP THE NEXT GENERATION OF CONSERVATIVE VOICES

While the public university is "politically neutral and apolitical," Anderson said it's important to provide a space to share varied viewpoints for the students' benefit.

"We don't jump in the fray, but we host the frays," he said.

"We allow people to come in and focus on civil dialogue, engaging in new and good ideas, and that's where we hope to excel," he continued. "A place that anyone can come with any idea, have a place for open, honest, violence-free debate, and that's what our future is, and that is what institutions of higher education are, when they are at their best."

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Kirk's suspected assassin, 23-year-old Tyler Robinson, pleaded not guilty to all charges through his attorneys at his arraignment on Sept. 1 — nearly a year after his arrest.

He's due back in court on Oct. 23, when Judge Tony Graf Jr. could set a trial date.

He could face the death penalty if convicted of the top charge of aggravated murder.

Kirk, 31, was married with two children.
